nameStory: The red stinkhorn gets its memorable name from two unmistakable features: its bright reddish-orange color and its absolutely awful smell. Like other stinkhorns, it produces a foul odor reminiscent of rotting meat to attract flies, which then spread its spores – nature's clever but smelly strategy for reproduction!
description: The red stinkhorn is one of nature's most bizarre-looking fungi, resembling a bright reddish-orange finger or small club poking up from the ground. This peculiar mushroom starts life as a white, egg-like structure buried in soil or leaf litter, then dramatically bursts forth as a hollow, spongy column. It typically reaches 3-6 inches tall and produces an unmistakable putrid odor that you'll smell before you see it. The entire structure has a porous, honeycomb-like texture that feels soft and slightly squishy to the touch.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Produces an intensely foul odor like rotting meat or garbage that can be detected from several feet away, especially on warm, humid days

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Emerges as a bright reddish-orange, finger-like column that's hollow inside with a spongy, honeycomb texture throughout

idTips.label: Egg Stage
idTips.description: Begins as a white or pinkish, egg-shaped structure about golf ball size that splits open to reveal the emerging stinkhorn

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and squishy like a kitchen sponge, with visible pores and chambers throughout the structure

idTips.label: Base
idTips.description: Remains of the white egg case often visible as a cup-like structure at the base of the mature fungus

idTips.label: Spores
idTips.description: Dark, slimy spore mass covers the tip initially but is quickly eaten by attracted flies, leaving a cleaner orange surface

habitat: Red stinkhorns thrive in rich, organic soil in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly where there's plenty of decaying leaf matter and wood debris. Look for them in shaded areas with good moisture retention, often near rotting logs, in mulched garden beds, or in areas with deep leaf litter. They're saprophytic fungi, meaning they feed on dead organic matter rather than living plants.

seasonality.spring: Egg cases may begin forming in late spring in warmer, protected locations with rich organic matter, though they're easily overlooked at this stage.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for red stinkhorns, especially after warm summer rains when the dramatic emergence from egg to full stinkhorn happens rapidly, often overnight.
seasonality.fall: Still actively fruiting in early fall, particularly during warm, humid periods following rain showers, before cold weather shuts down activity.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no visible fruiting bodies, though the underground mycelium remains alive in the soil waiting for warmer conditions.

funFact: Red stinkhorns can grow from egg to full size in just a few hours – you can literally watch them emerge and expand in real time, making them one of the fastest-growing organisms in New England forests!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with its close relative the devil's dipstick (Mutinus elegans), but the red stinkhorn has a more intensely reddish-orange color throughout, while devil's dipstick typically has a paler, more pinkish body with just a red tip. Memory trick: 'Red stinkhorn is red all around, devil's dipstick has red at the crown.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite their shocking appearance and smell, stinkhorns are completely harmless and actually beneficial decomposers in forest ecosystems. However, never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification – the 'egg' stage of stinkhorns is sometimes mistaken for edible puffballs by inexperienced foragers.
compareHints: Compared to its genus mate the devil's dipstick, the red stinkhorn maintains its bright reddish-orange color throughout the entire structure, while devil's dipstick tends to be paler with concentrated red coloring mainly at the tip. Both species have the same terrible smell and spongy texture, but the red stinkhorn's more uniform, intense coloration is the key distinguishing feature. Both emerge from similar white egg cases and prefer the same rich, organic habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Devil's dipstick differs from its close relative red stinkhorn mainly in its pointed tip versus the red stinkhorn's blunt, rounded end.
